1	# Body
2	
3	## KeyPoints
4	
5	Question Is service in the US military associated with suicide risk among those with disability?
6	
7	Findings In this survey study with selfreported cross-sectional data from 231 099 US adults, representing more than 236 million individuals, service in the military was associated with higher suicide risk among those without disability. However, among those with disability, military service was associated with lower suicide risk compared with nonveterans with disability.
8	
9	Meaning These findings suggest that military service could be a protective factor against suicide among a subpopulation of US adults.
10	
11	<!-- image -->
12	
13	## [+ Supplementalcontent](https://jama.jamanetwork.com/article.aspx?doi=10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.37679&utm_campaign=articlePDF%26utm_medium=articlePDFlink%26utm_source=articlePDF%26utm_content=jamanetworkopen.2023.37679)
14	
15	Author affiliations and article information are listed at the end of this article.
16	
17	<!-- image -->
18	
19	## Introduction
20	
21	Suicide is a leading public health concern. In 2020, there were nearly 46 000 suicide deaths with more than 1.2 million suicide attempts. 1 Suicide was listed as the 12th leading cause of death, at a rate of 13.48 per 100 000 people, with men at greatest risk. 1 Also in 2020, 4.9% of US adults reported suicide ideation, 1.3% suicide planning, and 0.5% attempting suicide. 2 Suicide and self-directed injury have high costs to society that extend beyond the emotional toll of losing individuals to a preventable cause of death. Notably, suicide behaviors cost more than $1.3 trillion/y in lifetime medical and work-loss expenditures. 3
22	
23	Amongthose at heightened risk for suicide are people with disability. Indeed, a recent US population-based study demonstrated that the presence of any disability impacting function was associated with a greater likelihood of reporting suicide ideation, suicide planning, and attempting suicide, with risk increasing as the number of disabling limitations increased. 4 Unfortunately, and as observed in the literature, 5 subgroups of people with disability at most heightened risk for death by suicide are not well known. Within the disability population, veterans of US military service are overrepresented, 6 likely due to exposure to injury and death during service. The most common physical disabilities among veterans include tinnitus, hearing loss, and motor deficits. 7 Veterans are also overrepresented in the population of individuals who die by suicide. In 2020, 6146 veterans died by suicide with an unadjusted rate of 31.7 per 100 000 people. 8 This is over twice the general US population suicide rate, 1 with elevated risk among veterans consistently observed over a 19-year period. 1 As of 2020, suicide was the 2nd leading cause of death among service members and veterans younger than 45 years, and the 13th leading cause among all veterans. 8 In sum, veterans are at greater risk for having a disability and for experiencing heightened risk for suicide relative to nonveterans. However, little is known about how veteran status may moderate the effect of disability status on risk for suicide-related outcomes.
24	
25	Although suicide risk in the context of disability has not been compared between veterans and nonveterans, critical within group differences have been observed among veterans. Veterans with disability (VWD) or physical health difficulties exhibited heightened suicide risk and were more likely to attempt suicide relative to veterans without disability. 9-14 However, among VWD, those who received lower or no disability-related benefits were at higher suicide risk, 15,16 and receipt of benefits mitigated risk for suicide. 17 Although existing studies highlight the complexity of disability and risk for suicide within military samples, current evidence has not directly compared risk of suicide-related outcomes between veteran and nonveteran samples with and without disabi

headline.statement: The paper's central conclusion -- that military service protects against suicide among people with disability -- rests on 3 of 15 veteran-vs-nonveteran contrasts reaching p <= .05, while the Discussion describes the pattern as "uniform" even though six of those fifteen point estimates run in the opposite direction.
headline.evidence: Discussion: "results were not uniform across all levels of risk for suicide and disability status, but were uniform among veteran status: being a US veteran mitigated the association of disability status and risk for suicide." Against this, the veteran-vs-nonveteran contrasts among people WITH disability in Table 2 are: 1 limitation -- ideation 0.83 (0.59-1.18), planning 0.57 (0.34-0.95), attempt 1.19 (0.70-2.04); 2 limitations -- ideation 1.25 (0.81-1.95), planning 1.03 (0.45-2.38), attempt 0.46 (0.24-0.88); >=3 limitations -- ideation 0.96 (0.58-1.58), planning 1.14 (0.65-2.03), attempt 0.68 (0.32-1.45). Table 3 adds: 1 limitation -- planning 0.61 (0.35-1.05), attempt 1.17 (0.63-2.18); 2 limitations -- planning 0.87 (0.37-2.04), attempt 0.31 (0.14-0.66); >=3 limitations -- planning 1.14 (0.58-2.25), attempt 0.75 (0.31-1.81). Only 0.57, 0.46 and 0.31 are significant; 1.19, 1.25, 1.03, 1.14, 1.17 and 1.14 point toward higher risk among veterans. The paper itself states "No significant differences in risks for suicide were observed by veteran status among people reporting 3 or more disabling limitations."

findings.title: Headline protective-effect claim generalizes well beyond the 3 of 15 subgroup contrasts that support it
findings.location: Key Points (Findings and Meaning); Abstract; Discussion paragraph 1; Tables 2 and 3
findings.reported: Key Points: "service in the military was associated with higher suicide risk among those without disability. However, among those with disability, military service was associated with lower suicide risk compared with nonveterans with disability." Discussion: results "were uniform among veteran status." Conclusions: "prior military service may be protective against suicide when considering disability status."
findings.computed: Enumerating every veteran-vs-nonveteran contrast among people with disability: 9 in Table 2 (2 significant -- planning at 1 limitation AOR 0.57, attempt at 2 limitations AOR 0.46) and 6 in Table 3 (1 significant -- attempt at 2 limitations AOR 0.31). That is 3 of 15. Six of the fifteen point estimates (1.19, 1.25, 1.03, 1.14, 1.17, 1.14) lie above 1.0, i.e. toward HIGHER risk among veterans with disability, directly contradicting "uniform." No contrast at >=3 limitations -- the most disabled group -- reaches significance, and the two significant Table 2 results fall at different disability levels for different outcomes with no gradient. On the elevated-risk side, 1 of 3 contrasts among people WITHOUT disability is significant (planning, AOR 1.71); ideation (1.12) and attempt (0.98) are flat. All three significant estimates were independently re-verified as internally consistent: 0.57 (0.34-0.95) recovers p = 0.0320 vs printed .03; 0.46 (0.24-0.88) recovers p = 0.0191 vs printed .02; 1.71 (1.17-2.49) recovers p = 0.0054 vs printed .006.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed tables. The counts are enumerations of rows in Tables 2 and 3 as printed, not recomputed statistics; every estimate quoted was cross-checked between the markdown and PDF extractions by the sweep. Every significant estimate does point in the claimed direction, so this is over-generalization of scope, not misstatement of direction, and the tables themselves report the numbers correctly.

findings.title: Moderation is asserted throughout but the disability x veteran interaction is never tested or reported
findings.location: Method, "Statistical Analysis"; Tables 2 and 3; Discussion; Conclusions
findings.reported: Method: "Multivariable adjusted multinomial logistic regression with an interaction term for disability status x veteran status estimated adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% CIs." Conclusions: "This study builds on the previous literature ... by exploring veteran status as a moderator." Introduction: "little is known about how veteran status may moderate the effect of disability status."
findings.computed: The interaction term is fitted but its coefficient, its confidence interval and its p-value appear nowhere in the paper. Tables 2 and 3 report only simple effects within strata: 50 AORs, all of them either veteran-vs-nonveteran at a fixed disability level or disability-level-vs-none within a fixed veteran group. The abstract's contrast -- higher risk without disability, lower risk with disability -- is a claim that two subgroup effects DIFFER, which is exactly what the untested interaction term estimates. The claimed reversal is inferred from AOR 1.71 (p = .006) at no limitations versus AOR 0.57 (p = .03) at 1 limitation; the two intervals (1.17-2.49 and 0.34-0.95) are compared only by their significance status. This is the difference-in-significance error (Gelman & Stern): the difference between a significant and a non-significant result, or between two significant results of opposite sign, is not itself established without a test of the difference.
findings.assumptions: Assumes the interaction test is genuinely absent from the main text rather than reported only in Supplement 1, which was not available for this review. The Method describes an interaction model and the paper's central claim is a moderation claim, so its omission from the primary tables is the finding regardless of what the supplement contains. No tool in this suite tests an interaction from published subgroup estimates; the observation rests on reading the Method against Tables 2 and 3.

findings.title: Claims are arbitrated by an unverifiable sensitivity analysis that imputes both the outcome and the exposure
findings.location: Method, "Statistical Analysis"; Results paragraphs on eTables 3 and 4; Supplement 1 (not provided)
findings.reported: "Sensitivity analyses were performed with multiple imputation by chained equations for all missing values to assess bias." Results: "veterans were 71% more likely to report planning relative to nonveterans (AOR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.17-2.49) (Table 2), but this was not significant in sensitivity analyses." Also: "nonveterans reporting 3 or more disabilities were 102% more likely to report attempt in sensitivity analyses only" and "nonveterans reporting 3 or more disabling limitations were more likely to report planning in sensitivity analyses" and "veterans with 1 disabling limitation were more likely to report planning ... but this finding was only significant in sensitivity analyses."
findings.computed: eTable 3 runs on N = 241 675 against 231 099 in the main analysis -- 10 576 records restored by imputation. Per the paper's own flow diagram this necessarily includes imputing the OUTCOME (suicide ideation/planning/attempt) for 1141 respondents and the EXPOSURE (disability status) for 2044, alongside 130 missing veteran status and 7261 missing covariates. Imputing the dependent variable adds no information about the outcome-predictor association while propagating the imputation model's assumptions into the estimate; imputing the exposure compounds it. This matters more than usual here because at least four reported claims turn on disagreements between the two analyses, in both directions: one Key-Points-supporting result loses significance under imputation, and three results are reported as findings on the strength of being significant under imputation ONLY. The imputation model is never described, and eTables 3-4 were not available, so the magnitude cannot be established.
findings.assumptions: The composition of the 10 576 imputed records is read off the paper's flow diagram, whose five exclusion counts plus the final sample were verified to reconcile exactly to 315 661 with zero residual. Severity is capped at suspicious and confidence at medium because Supplement 1 was not provided; the imputation specification could be documented there. Credit where due: the authors disclosed the non-replication of AOR 1.71 rather than suppressing it.

findings.title: One Table 3 average marginal effect is internally inconsistent with its own interval and p-value
findings.location: Table 3, Nonveteran / >=3 Limitations, suicide attempt (vs suicidal ideation only), AME column
findings.computed: The AME fails on two independent grounds. (1) The point estimate 0.04 is not the arithmetic midpoint of its interval [-0.01, 0.05]; the implied centre is 0.0200. Even allowing full 2-dp rounding on all three printed values, the attainable midpoint range does not reach the estimate's rounding range. (2) The p recovered from that interval is 0.0090 (SE 0.0153, z = 2.61), contradicting the p = .07 printed on the same row. The AOR on the SAME row was run as a control and is fully self-consistent: 1.36 (0.98 to 1.89) recovers p = 0.0665 against printed .07, sitting at its log-scale midpoint of 1.361. Two further Table 3 AMEs were re-checked as controls and behave normally -- the adjacent planning cell 0.04 (-0.01 to 0.10) centres at 0.045, and -0.11 (-0.18 to -0.04) p = .002 recovers p = 0.0021 exactly. The error is therefore localised to the printed AME interval, not to the fitted model; a single mis-set digit in the upper bound (0.05 for 0.09) would reconcile the row.
findings.assumptions: Assumes the AME is a probability difference with a null of 0, as the paper's own abbreviation list implies ("AME, average marginal effect"). Reported as suspicious rather than impossible: 0.04 does lie inside [-0.01, 0.05], so no arithmetic law is violated, and a transcription or typesetting error is the most parsimonious reading. The cell was confirmed in both the markdown and PDF extractions before flagging, which matters because Table 2 is typeset rotated and extracts mirror-reversed. Warrants a correction request rather than any stronger inference.

findings.title: No multiplicity correction across at least 68 tests, with the supporting results clustered at .02 to .04
findings.reported: "Test-specific significance levels were assessed at a <= .05." No correction of any kind is described.
findings.computed: At least 68 tests are enumerable in the main tables alone: 50 AORs across Tables 2 and 3 plus 18 bivariate comparisons in Table 1, before counting four supplementary eTables. The veteran-vs-nonveteran contrasts carrying the abstract form a family of 12 in Table 2 and 8 in Table 3. Within either family, a Bonferroni-type adjustment would retain only the strongest result (AOR 0.31, p = .002) and drop the rest, including both Table 2 results the Key Points rest on (p = .03 and p = .02) and the Table 3 subgroup result (AOR 1.61, p = .04). Six headline-supporting claims have p between .01 and .04.
findings.assumptions: This is an enumeration of the paper's own reported tests; no adjusted threshold was computed. Uncorrected reporting is common and accepted in descriptive epidemiology and is not an error in itself -- it is reported because of which conclusions it bears on, given that the supporting results sit within a factor of two of the threshold and the study is explicitly exploratory (no preregistration, no stated hypothesis, no power analysis).

findings.title: The stated null at 3 or more limitations rests on intervals compatible with three-fold effects in either direction
findings.location: Results, "Suicide Ideation, Planning, and Attempt by Veteran and Disability Status", final sentence; Table 2
findings.reported: "No significant differences in risks for suicide were observed by veteran status among people reporting 3 or more disabling limitations." Underlying intervals: ideation 0.96 (0.58 to 1.58) p = .87; planning 1.14 (0.65 to 2.03) p = .65; attempt 0.68 (0.32 to 1.45) p = .32.
findings.computed: All three intervals include the null but remain compatible with substantial effects in BOTH directions: up to 1.72-fold for ideation, 2.03-fold for planning and 3.13-fold for attempt. The attempt interval [0.32, 1.45] is especially uninformative -- equally compatible with veterans having roughly a third the odds of attempt and with half again the odds. The tool returns indeterminate because the paper states no smallest effect size of interest, so equivalence cannot be tested; that refusal is the result. The paper concedes the cause in its own Limitations: "due to smaller cell sizes after stratifying sample groups to veteran and nonveterans."
findings.assumptions: The sentence as written is defensible -- it says "no significant differences", not "no differences". It is reported because this is the boundary condition on the Key Points' unqualified protective claim: the subgroup where a protective effect would matter most is the one where the study has least power, and the Key Points do not carry that qualification. No SESOI was assumed; none is stated.

not_checked.location: Supplement 1, eTables 1-4 (bivariate characteristics by suicide outcome and by disability status; multiple-imputation sensitivity analyses for both models)
not_checked.reason: The supplement was not provided with the paper files. This is the single largest coverage gap. eTables 1-2 contain the bivariate associations the paper says drove covariate selection ("All evaluated covariates had significant bivariate associations"); eTables 3-4 contain the sensitivity analyses on which several reported claims depend -- including one Key-Points-supporting result that did NOT replicate (AOR 1.71) and at least three results reported as significant ONLY under imputation. None of those numbers could be verified.

not_checked.location: Table 1, the 18 bivariate P values (recalculation from cell counts)
not_checked.reason: Unweighted cell counts are never printed -- only weighted percentages and weighted population totals. A design-based Rao-Scott test on a stratified multistage cluster sample cannot be reproduced from weighted marginals alone, and recalc_chi_squared assumes simple random sampling, so applying it would test a different hypothesis than the one the paper reports.

not_checked.location: Table 2, the 30 average marginal effects (AME column)
not_checked.reason: Almost all are printed as 0, 0.01, 0.02 or 0.03 with intervals such as "0 (0 to 0)" and "0 (-0.01 to 0.01)". At that precision the midpoint and p-recovery checks have essentially no resolving power -- the rounding interval swamps the quantity being tested. Table 3's AMEs are printed to 2 decimals with wider intervals and WERE checked; that is where the one genuine AME anomaly was found.

not_checked.location: GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE, DEBIT and 2x2 reconstruction across the whole paper
not_checked.reason: Deliberately not applied. Every percentage in Table 1 is survey-weighted: its denominator is a sum of sampling weights, not a count of people, so a weighted percentage is not of the form k/n and GRIM-family granularity arguments do not hold. The paper reports no means and no standard deviations anywhere, so GRIMMER and SPRITE have no input. Applying these tools here would manufacture impossibilities from entirely ordinary cells.

not_checked.location: Effect-size plausibility benchmarking of the headline odds ratios
not_checked.reason: check_effect_plausibility requires group means and SDs, or a Cohen's d. This paper reports neither -- its outcomes are categorical and its effects are adjusted odds ratios from a survey-weighted multinomial model. No field benchmark in the tool's cited set applies, so the check was declined rather than forced.

not_checked.location: Independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA) and other distributional assumptions of the multinomial models
not_checked.reason: The authors report checking multicollinearity by variance inflation factor and state it was not detected; they report no check of IIA, which multinomial logistic regression assumes. No tool in this suite tests IIA, and an unreported assumption check is not by itself a finding.

not_checked.location: Ratio of the reported 8.92% veteran share to the unweighted counts n = 13 859 / 231 099
not_checked.reason: The phrase "8.92% of the sample" is the WEIGHTED population share, whereas the unweighted analytic-sample share implied by those counts is materially lower. Both figures are printed side by side so nothing is hidden, and every summation check on them passes. Confirming the intended denominator requires dividing one reported count by another; no validated tool in this suite performs ratio arithmetic, and it was not computed by hand. Recorded as an ambiguity for human verification.

limitations: This agent reads text and tables only. It does not see figures. The study cohort flowchart was checked from its transcribed counts, not from the rendered image, and any information carried only by a plotted mark was invisible to this review.

Supplement 1 (eTables 1-4) was not provided. Several of the paper's reported claims are adjudicated by those sensitivity analyses, and none of their numbers could be verified. Finding 3 is bounded by this gap and is reported at medium confidence for that reason.

Table 2 is typeset rotated in the source PDF and extracts mirror-reversed, while the markdown version arrives transposed with scrambled column headers. Both extractions were reconciled cell by cell before any check ran and agreed on all 50 estimates, but a transcription error in a rotated table is a standard route to a false accusation and residual risk cannot be driven to zero.

P-values recovered from confidence intervals use a normal approximation. The paper used SAS PROC SURVEY on a stratified multistage cluster sample, where Wald intervals use a t-multiplier on design degrees of freedom rather than 1.96. Discrepancies smaller than one unit in the last printed decimal are therefore uninformative here and were not treated as findings.
The interaction-test finding (rank 2) rests on reading the Method against Tables 2 and 3, not on a tool: no check in this suite reconstructs an interaction test from published subgroup estimates.

No statement is made about whether the substantive conclusions are true. The checks establish only whether the reported numbers are mutually consistent and whether the stated conclusions follow from the reported estimates.

input.report_markdown:
This is a secondary analysis of six pooled years (2015-2020) of the National Survey on Drug Use and Health: 231 099 adults, weighted to 236 551 727 US adults, analysed in SAS PROC SURVEY with person-level weights, strata and PSU clusters. A multinomial logistic model regresses a four-level suicide outcome (none / ideation only / planning without attempt / attempt) on number of disabling limitations, veteran status and their interaction, adjusted for eighteen covariates. A subgroup model repeats the analysis among those reporting ideation. The authors conclude that military service is associated with higher suicide risk among adults without disability and lower risk among adults with disability -- that veteran status is a protective moderator.

Start with what is right, because it constrains how everything else should be read. The arithmetic in this paper is unusually clean, and I found no sign of a data-integrity problem. The cohort flow reconciles exactly: five exclusion counts plus the final sample account for all 315 661 NSDUH respondents with zero residual. All fifty odds ratios sit at the log-scale midpoint of their own intervals -- the correct symmetry test for a ratio measure, and one that misfires on roughly a third of ratio estimates if done on the linear scale. Not one fails it. All 36 Table 1 percentage column sums reach 100% within rounding; seven of ten weighted-N blocks sum to the stated total with zero residual and the other three miss by one unit, which is what independently rounded survey-weighted population estimates do. Text and tables agree where they overlap. No duplicated estimate pairs across 600 comparisons, no round-N signature, and the underlying NSDUH data are genuinely public, so there is no state-but-withhold problem. The three estimates the conclusions lean on all reconcile with both their intervals and their printed p-values.

Several sweep flags do not survive that context and I am not carrying them. Nine of fifty odds ratios have a p recovered from their own interval differing from the printed p -- but in every case by less than 0.016, under one unit in the second decimal at which these are printed, and the direction is mixed (four up, five down). A paper shifting p-values toward significance would not look like that. More decisively, recovery assumes a normal approximation while the paper used design-based Wald intervals with a t-multiplier on design degrees of freedom; that alone displaces recovered p at this magnitude. This is reporting precision, not an integrity signal. I also discard the STALT flag on the twelve rows printed as P < .001: recovered z runs from 6.7 to 13.4, which is the ordinary consequence of 231 099 respondents acting on genuinely large disability-suicide associations, and nothing is concealed because the odds ratio and its interval are printed alongside. Escalating that would be a textbook false positive on a large-N epidemiological paper. One interval whose width reads more like 90% than 95% is a single occurrence among fifty on a near-null estimate and is noise. A cross-reference to eTable 3 that should read eTable 4 is a typographical slip affecting no number.

One deprioritization deserves to be explicit, because it is where this class of review most often goes wrong. All eighteen Table 1 p-values are at or below .006 -- uniformly LOW. The Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher and Bayesian dispersion tests detect the opposite pattern, groups more similar than randomisation permits, and both presuppose random allocation. Nothing was randomised here. Veteran status is a self-reported characteristic and the groups are expected to differ profoundly, as they do: 91.0% versus 44.0% male, 48.8% versus 17.8% aged 65 or over. Uniformly low baseline p-values are the substantive result that motivated covariate adjustment, not a red flag, and the rulebook's under-dispersion signature is not definable in this design. Running either test would have been a category error. The sweep declined correctly.

What remains is not an arithmetic problem but an inferential one, and it is why the verdict is questionable rather than trustworthy. The distinction matters: I do not doubt these numbers. I doubt that they support the sentence in the Key Points. The paper fits an interaction model, never reports the interaction, and then reads a moderation conclusion off the significance status of simple effects within strata -- three of fifteen of which reach the threshold, with six of the fifteen pointing the other way, in a family of at least 68 uncorrected tests, with the disagreements between the main and imputed analyses resolved in whichever direction reaches .05. The single internally inconsistent cell in Table 3 is a typo-grade error on a non-headline result and I rank it below all of that deliberately; it warrants a correction notice, nothing more.

The data appear sound and the reported statistics very largely verify. The conclusions drawn from them are considerably stronger than the tables support, and the Discussion's characterisation of the pattern as "uniform" should be corrected.
